chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
title: The layman, the back beat and a freedom radio program
summary: The working listener just wants the beat; Sam switches off a WBGO announcer who plays only freedom music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: See he parked his finger in there because that back beat is there and he could pop his finger and he'd pat his feet and he could get up and shake his butt man and do anything he wanted to do because that beat is not going anywhere, you see. And all of that conversation while we was talking lead us right back to what's going on now, man, to what's going on now. You see because it all is on the layman.

Me and you and her, we know what these guys are doing. They're going crazy jumping all up and down on the instruments and stuff. We understand it because we play too. But the dude that don't play, the guy that put the bread in the kitchen, he don't hear that shit man, you know.

All he wants to do is park his finger man. He's got his girl. He's now out on the weekend there. He done work 8 hours a day. Boy he don't want to hear that shit man. He's going ahead. He don't want to hear that other, all that hollering and squeaking and carrying on and all that. I heard on W...one of the stations, WBLS? BLS No, WBGO. It's one disk jockey that comes on. He played nothing but Freedom.
Have you ever heard it? Have you heard him?
I haven't heard. I missed here.

I'm a musician man. I'll be sitting here, man. Gee I can get up and change the channel, man. You know because that gets to me, man. I tell you just sit here man and listen to that Freedom for 3 hours man, you know. And I'm a musician. I can't stand that shit you know. And some of that, this guy, he don't play nothing. His whole program was that. I can't think of his name. I forgot his name. I don't want to even remember his name. But I have to get up and cut that shit off, you know.
